teaser: Eight hours of combat, dozens of lances, and not one drop of blood.
review_notes:
Battle of San Romano, 1 June 1432, Florence against Siena; duration 'about eight hours' follows the National Gallery's account.
London panel about 182 x 320 cm; date c. 1438-40.
Commissioned by Lionardo Bartolini Salimbeni; later taken by Lorenzo de' Medici, with one co-owner's share removed by force (documents published by F. Caglioti); date around 1484.
Panels originally had arched tops, later cut and squared.
Armor laid in silver leaf, now tarnished and abraded.
Vasari's anecdote about Uccello's wife and perspective is paraphrased, not quoted.
Uccello's early training in Ghiberti's workshop.
National Gallery acquired the panel in 1857.
The page is described only as bareheaded; the National Gallery says he carries his master's helmet, not legible in this image.

lesson.text: Three. That is how many paintings Paolo Uccello needed for a single day of fighting, and how many cities you must visit now to see it whole: London, Florence and Paris. This is the London panel, 3.2 meters wide (about 10.5 feet), where the battle begins.

The day was June 1, 1432. Florence and its rival Siena clashed at San Romano, in the valley between them. The Florentine commander, Niccolò da Tolentino, was caught with a small force and held on until help arrived. Florence called it a glorious win. Siena did not see it that way.

The real fight is said to have lasted about eight hours. Niccolò was a condottiere, a general for hire, and battles between such professionals were often long, noisy and surprisingly light on deaths: a captured knight was worth a ransom.

So where is the commander? The left half of the panel is a crush of steel helmets, visors down, each one as anonymous as the next. Uccello makes his hero easy to spot by breaking every rule of battlefield safety.

lesson.title: The charge
lesson.text: The Florentines pour in from the left. Their leader is at the center.

spots.title: A hat, in a battle
spots.text: Niccolò rides with no helmet. He wears a huge red and gold hat of patterned silk and points his baton forward. This is a portrait of command, not a report of what he wore that day.

spots.title: The white horse
spots.text: His horse rears with both forelegs up, smooth and rounded like a carousel animal. Gold discs stud its red harness. Uccello cares more for its clean shape than for veins or sweat.

spots.title: The page
spots.text: Just behind him rides a bareheaded boy with blond curls and a calm, pale face, his young attendant. Among the iron masks, the only two human faces belong to the hero and this child.

spots.title: Trumpets
spots.text: Long brass trumpets cut across the lances. The picture has a soundtrack: horns, hooves, metal. But the men blowing them are almost hidden. You see the noise, not the players.

lesson.text: A fancy hat, a child at his side, a toy-like horse: this is war as pageant. The panels were not made for a town hall. A rich Florentine, Lionardo Bartolini Salimbeni, ordered them for his own house, where they lined a room like the most expensive wallpaper in the city.

Uccello had another passion to serve besides his client. He was obsessed with perspective, the brand-new geometry that lets a flat picture look deep by making parallel lines run toward a single point. Drop your eyes to the pink ground, to the mess the battle has left behind.
Broken lances lie where they fell. Or do they?

lines.label: A lance on the left
lines.text: Extend this fallen lance and it heads up and inward, toward the middle of the picture.

lines.label: A lance on the right
lines.text: This one leans the other way and aims at the same zone, near the white horse. The debris is laid out like the lines of a tiled floor running into depth.

lines.label: The fallen knight
lines.text: Even the casualty obeys. He lies face down with his feet toward us and his head pointing into the picture, squeezed short by the angle. That squeezing is called foreshortening.

lesson.text: Nothing here dropped at random. Uccello arranged the wreckage of a battle into a drawing lesson, and used a dead soldier as a ruler. He was one of the first to show a body lying straight into depth like this, a problem painters would wrestle with for a century.
His biographer Giorgio Vasari tells that Uccello sat up all night over perspective problems. When his wife called him to bed, he would only answer how sweet a thing perspective was.
Uccello treats the battlefield as a geometry problem. The foreground is a measured stage, and every broken lance is there to prove that paint can make depth.

Then the geometry stops. Above the hedge of roses and orange trees, the land does not recede. It stands up like a painted backdrop, and the fields look like pale stripes. Up there, far from the knights, a smaller kind of fighting goes on.
Not everyone has a horse. Find the foot soldiers still running and fighting in the distance.

spots.title: The foot soldiers
spots.text: Tiny men in bright hose dash along the slope. One bends to reload a crossbow, others swing pikes, two riders climb the path. They are far too small for their distance and seem to belong to another picture.

lesson.text: Two ways of painting share one panel. In front, the new science of the 1430s. Behind, the older taste of tapestries and illustrated books, where a hill is a pattern and figures are scattered for charm. Uccello had trained in a workshop that loved such decoration, and he never gave it up.

“Uccello” means “bird.” The painter was born Paolo di Dono, and the nickname came from his love of painting birds and other animals. He is said to have filled his house with pictures of them because he could not afford the real ones.

One thing you cannot see anymore changes everything. The armor was covered in real silver leaf, hammered thin and polished. It has tarnished to the gray-brown you see now. Picture the room by candlelight around 1440: dozens of knights glittering like mirrors, gold flashing on the harness.

spots.title: Tarnished silver
spots.text: These plates were once bright silver leaf with painted shadows on top. Time has dulled the metal, so the knights now look darker and flatter than Uccello meant.

spots.title: Oranges
spots.text: Ripe oranges glow among dark leaves behind the lances. The fruit is as round and tidy as the gold studs on the horses, another excuse for a perfect shape.

spots.title: Roses in the hedge
spots.text: White and pink roses bloom along the hedge that walls off the fight. A battle in a garden: the mood is closer to a tournament than to a massacre.

spots.title: An empty helmet
spots.text: A helmet lies on the pink ground, drawn carefully in the round. Uccello loved such objects for the puzzle of their curves. Its owner is nowhere to be seen.

spots.title: The banner
spots.text: Niccolò's white standard streams above the charge, its long tails curling against the hill. It tells the viewer whose victory this room is meant to celebrate.

spots.title: The gray horse
spots.text: On the right a pale horse turns in blue and gold harness. Horses in white, black, gray and brown alternate across the panel like pieces set out on a board.

lesson.text: The pictures were too good to stay put. Decades later Lorenzo de' Medici, the most powerful man in Florence, wanted all three for his palace. One of the heirs refused to give up his share, and Lorenzo's men simply carried the panels off.

They were trimmed to fit their new walls: the tops were once arched, and the corners were later filled in to make rectangles. In the nineteenth century the set was split up for good. The London panel arrived at the National Gallery in 1857.

People still argue about what kind of painter this makes Uccello. A stiff storyteller who could not make a battle move? Or someone who saw that lances, hooves and helmets could become pure pattern, five hundred years before abstract art? Stand in front of the pink floor and decide.

quiz.question: Which two cities fought at San Romano in 1432?
quiz.explanation: Florence, led by Niccolò da Tolentino, fought its rival Siena.

quiz.question: How does Uccello make the commander stand out?
options: He is twice the size of the others
He alone rides a black horse
He wears a big red and gold hat and no helmet
quiz.explanation: Niccolò rides bareheaded in a silk hat, a portrait of command.

quiz.question: What do the broken lances on the ground do?
options: They point into depth like lines of perspective
They mark where each soldier died
quiz.explanation: Uccello arranged them to run toward the center, building depth.

quiz.question: What was the knights' armor originally covered with?
quiz.explanation: Real silver leaf, which has since tarnished to gray-brown.

quiz.question: What is foreshortening?
options: Showing a body squeezed short because it points into depth
Cutting a panel to fit a wall
quiz.explanation: The fallen knight is shortened because he lies straight into the picture.

quiz.question: Who had the panels carried off to his own palace?
quiz.explanation: Lorenzo de' Medici wanted all three and took them.

facts.text: The three San Romano panels hang together in one museum.
facts.explanation: They are split between London, Florence and Paris.
Paolo di Dono earned it through his love of painting birds and animals.

facts.text: The panels were first made for a public town hall.
facts.explanation: A wealthy Florentine ordered them for a room in his own house.
